subject: math
description: Students distinguish correlation from causation. Given a scatterplot, a correlation coefficient $r$, or a described association between two variables, they decide whether the data supports a claim that one variable causes a change in the other. They explain why a strong correlation alone does not establish causation, identify plausible confounding (lurking) variables, recognize reverse causation and coincidence, and state that only a well-designed randomized controlled experiment can justify a causal conclusion. They also interpret the sign and approximate strength of $r$ where $-1 \le r \le 1$ as it relates to association, not cause.
subSkills: Read the direction and strength of an association from a scatterplot or a correlation coefficient $r$ (with $-1 \le r \le 1$)
State that correlation measures association, not cause, and explain why
Identify a plausible confounding (lurking) variable that could produce an observed correlation
Recognize reverse causation (the effect could run the other way)
Recognize coincidental correlation (no real mechanism linking the variables)
Distinguish an observational study from a randomized controlled experiment and explain why only the latter can establish causation
Evaluate and critique a causal claim made from correlational data

problemArchetypes.name: Correlation does not imply causation (identify the flaw)
problemArchetypes.example: A study finds that towns with more firefighters tend to have more fire damage, with $r = 0.86$. A reporter concludes that firefighters cause fire damage. Identify the lurking variable and explain why the causal claim is unjustified. (Answer: fire size is the confounder; larger fires draw more firefighters and cause more damage.)

problemArchetypes.name: Name the confounding (lurking) variable
problemArchetypes.example: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are positively correlated. Name a lurking variable that explains both. (Answer: hot weather / summer temperature increases both ice cream sales and swimming.)

problemArchetypes.name: Reverse causation
problemArchetypes.example: Researchers note a negative correlation between hours of exercise per week and resting heart rate. A claim states that a low heart rate causes people to exercise more. Explain why the direction of causation could plausibly be reversed. (Answer: exercising more lowers resting heart rate, so the causal arrow likely runs the other way.)

problemArchetypes.name: Coincidence vs. real association
problemArchetypes.example: Over ten years, the number of films a particular actor appears in is correlated with national cheese consumption at $r = 0.94$. Decide whether this supports a causal link and justify. (Answer: coincidental; no plausible mechanism, so high $r$ does not imply cause.)

problemArchetypes.name: Observational study vs. randomized experiment
problemArchetypes.example: Two designs are described for testing whether a tutoring program raises test scores: (a) compare students who chose to enroll with those who did not, or (b) randomly assign students to tutoring or no tutoring. Which design can support a causal conclusion and why? (Answer: (b); random assignment balances confounders so a difference can be attributed to the program.)

problemArchetypes.name: Interpret $r$ as association, not cause
problemArchetypes.example: A scatterplot of study time vs. exam score has $r = 0.78$. State what $r$ tells you and what it does not. (Answer: a fairly strong positive linear association; it does not prove that studying more causes higher scores, since other factors may be involved.)

Easy.description: One-step recognition. Student reads the sign/strength of an association or applies the single rule 'correlation is not causation' to a clear, familiar context. Only one cause-vs-association judgment is required and the lurking variable (if any) is obvious.
constraints: Familiar everyday context (ice cream, weather, exercise, sleep)
Either interpret the sign of $r$ OR judge a single causal claim true/false, not both
Any lurking variable is obvious and commonly known
No comparison of study designs required

Medium.description: Student must name the specific type of flaw (confounding, reverse causation, or coincidence) and justify it, OR identify a plausible lurking variable that is not obvious. May combine reading $r$ with judging a causal claim.
constraints: Student must classify WHY the causal claim fails (lurking variable / reverse causation / coincidence), not just say it fails
Lurking variable requires some reasoning to surface
May ask student to interpret the strength of $r$ and the causal status together
Context may be less familiar (economics, health, demographics)

Hard.description: Multi-step evaluation. Student compares an observational study to a randomized controlled experiment, designs or critiques a study that could establish causation, or analyzes a scenario with more than one competing explanation and must rank or rule them out with justification.
constraints: Requires distinguishing observational data from a randomized controlled experiment
Student must explain HOW random assignment removes confounding, or propose such a design
Scenario admits multiple competing explanations that must be weighed
Answer is a written justification, not a single word

difficultyRubric.tierSplit: This standard is conceptual and answerable in a single ramped worksheet, so the default single sheet is used (15 items, Easy early to Hard late). If split: tier1 (Easy to Medium) covers reading $r$, the basic 'correlation is not causation' rule, and naming an obvious lurking variable; tier2 (Medium to Hard) covers classifying the flaw type, reverse causation, coincidence, and observational-vs-randomized-experiment reasoning. No item overlap.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Believes a strong correlation proves causation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasons that because $r$ is close to $1$ (e.g. $r = 0.9$), one variable must be causing the other, so the causal claim is justified.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Thinks a small or zero correlation means the variables cannot be causally related at all
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasons that since $r \approx 0$, there is definitely no relationship of any kind, ignoring nonlinear association or causation masked by other factors.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses the sign of $r$ with the presence/absence of causation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasons that a negative $r$ means there is no causation while a positive $r$ means there is, treating the sign as a cause indicator rather than a direction-of-association indicator.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Fails to consider a confounding (lurking) variable
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Accepts that the two correlated variables directly cause each other and overlooks a third variable that drives both.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Assumes causation runs in only one direction without checking reverse causation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Concludes A causes B from the correlation, never considering that B could just as plausibly cause A.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Treats an observational study as if it could establish causation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims that comparing self-selected groups (e.g. people who chose to enroll vs. those who did not) proves the treatment caused the difference, ignoring that confounders were not controlled by random assignment.
Reasons that since correlation never implies causation, the association must be meaningless coincidence, even when a plausible mechanism or a controlled experiment exists.

_comment_itemCounts: Conceptual reasoning standard. Quiz items are multiple choice with one defensible best answer; distractors embody the misconceptions above. Single ramped worksheet (no tier split).
